expected.question_text: An eight-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with new-onset cough and fever. His mother complains that he had a sudden-onset high fever (to 103.0°F) and productive cough that began one day ago. Additionally, the patient’s mother complains that he has been fatigued and has had daily nosebleeds for the past two weeks. Physical examination reveals tachycardia, a temperature of 39.3°C (102.8°F), pallor, lymphadenopathy, several bruises on the extremities and torso, and crackles in the right lower lobe. Laboratory studies reveal: | Platelet count | 85,000 u/L | 130,000-400,000u/L | |---|---|---| | Hemoglobin | 8 g/dL | 14.0-18.0 g/dL | | Hematocrit | 24% | 42%-52% | | Leukocyte count | 24,000/mm^3 | 4,800-10,800/mm^3 | Bone marrow biopsy stains with sudan black and peripheral blood smear is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following congenital childhood illnesses is most likely associated with this patient’s illness?
expected.explanation_footer:
Acute myelogenous leukemia, or AML, is a hematopoietic malignancy characterized by overproduction of blast cells that accumulate in the marrow and lead to abnormal production of other blood cells. The clinical presentation of AML is related primarily to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis with symptoms of fatigue, weakness, and dyspnea as well as easy bleeding and bruising. Young patients also often present with acute infection and high fever. Bone marrow biopsy will reveal auer rods within the cytoplasm of the leukemic blasts. AML is the most common leukemia in patients above the age of 30. When it presents in childhood, it is often associated with another illness or syndrome. One such congenital illness that can be associated with childhood AML is Fanconi anemia. AML is characterized by bone marrow infiltration with malignant cells in the myeloid blood cell line. Pancytopenia associated with AML results in increased infections, bleeding, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Leukocyte count can also be very high on complete blood count. Bone marrow biopsy will reveal blasts from the myeloid cell lineage (called myeloblasts) and will have reactions with myeloperoxidase and Sudan black. A classic finding also associated with AML on bone marrow biopsy is the presence of Auer rods within the cytoplasm of the myeloblasts. This is seen in the attached image. AML is much more commonly diagnosed in the adult population, and it is in fact the most common leukemia in adults above age 30. When encountered in a child, especially on examinations, AML tends to be accompanying another childhood illness. Look for patients with a history of Bloom syndrome (short stature, history of other cancers), Down syndrome (trisomy 21, cognitive impairment, short stature, slanted eyes, single palmar crease), neurofibromatosis (learning disabilities, multiple nervous tissue tumors), or Fanconi anemia. Fanconi anemia, which is caused by mutation of DNA repair genes, manifests in most children between ages six and nine years. Patients with Fanconi anemia usually have short stature; café au lait spots; and anomalies involving the thumb, radius, and genitourinary tract. The disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive or X-linked fashion. These patients have aplastic anemia (characterized by pancytopenia—low white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets—and bone marrow hypocellularity). Achondroplasia (choice A) is a skeletal dysplastic disease that causes the normal development of the head and neck, but stunts the growth of the limbs. Though it can be genetic and follows an autosomal dominant pattern, most cases actually arise spontaneously. Achondroplastic dwarfism occurs when there is a mutation in the FGFR3 gene, which lies on chromosome 4. The mutated DNA in the FGFR3 gene codes for a reduced amount of chondrocytes (cartilage-producing cells) on the epiphyseal plate of the growing bone. Cartilage plays a significant role in bone production because it is the precursor connective tissue that undergoes ossification to produce mature bone tissue. In dwarfism, ossification is successful in bones of the head and neck because the amount of chondroblasts is within the normal range. However, due to the FGFR3 gene mutation, the chondroblast count in the epiphyseal plates of the limbs is significantly lower, which translates to less bone tissue formation, and therefore, shorter limbs. Cystic fibrosis (choice B) is a genetic disease that has effects on multiple organ systems including the lungs, sinuses, and digestive tract. The major pathophysiologic mechanism in cystic fibrosis is deranged transport of chloride due to genetic mutation to the cystic fibrosis transmembrance conductance regulator (CFTR) genes. Clinical manifestations of cystic fibrosis include chronic respiratory disease, sinus disease, pancreatic insufficiency, and male infertility (through congenital absence of the vas deferens). A classic infant presentation of cystic fibrosis is meconium ileus (inability to pass the first stool due to thickened meconium). Children with cystic fibrosis tend also to exhibit failure to thrive with greasy, fatty stools as their pancreatic insufficiency leads to intestinal malabsorption. The average life expectancy of a patient with cystic fibrosis in the United States is 37 years of age. Marfan syndrome (choice D) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder of the connective tissue. This is due to a defect in the fibrillin gene which results in abnormal connective tissue. Look for long limbs, pectus excavatum (sunken-in chest), arachnodactyly (long and thin digits), and cardiac abnormalities. The most common cardiac anomaly associated with Marfan syndrome is mitral valve prolapse. Physical examination will reveal a mid-systolic click followed by a late-systolic murmur. Tay-Sachs disease (choice E) is an autosomal recessive sphingolipidosis. Tay-Sachs is caused by a defect in hexosaminidase A, which leads to a buildup o f GM2 gangliosides, especially in neurons. Deposits lead to developmental delay (severe cognitive delay) and progressive neurodegeneration (with weakness/hypotonia), which delays motor development. Tay-Sachs can present with a cherry-red spot on the macula. Lysosomes classically display “onion skinning.” Progression of the disease is rapid and death usually occurs by age four. Mnemonic: Tay-SaX (Tay-Sachs) lacks heXosaminidase.

Acute myelogenous leukemia is a hematopoietic malignancy characterized by bone marrow infiltration with malignant cells in the myeloid blood cell line. When seen in childhood, AML is often associated with other accompanying childhood diseases. One such illness that is linked to childhood AML is Fanconi anemia.
